topics.justification: Dominated by “sign” and “private_key”, plus “string/datum” and “method”, suggesting discussions about how to sign data and what exactly gets signed.
Words like “read”, “theory”, “design”, “concept”, and “paper/attack” point to learning-oriented posts about understanding cryptographic ideas and threat models from literature.
High weight on “key”, “verify/verification”, “store”, “secure”, and “random” indicates best practices around key management and verification steps (often contrasted with passwords/salts).

topics.topic_name: Cipher modes and secure usage guidance
topics.justification: The presence of “mode”, “secure”, “recommend”, and “understand” suggests conceptual Q&A on which modes to use and how to reason about secure configurations.
Terms like “wrong”, “clarify”, “reason”, “fact”, and “community” fit threads where answers explain why an assumption is incorrect and clarify common misunderstandings.
Centered on “hash”, “slow”, “salt”, “password”, and “store”, which strongly signals discussions of password storage, KDFs, and why slow hashing matters.

topics.topic_name: Security principles and separation from source code
topics.justification: Words like “security”, “provide”, “separate”, “source_code”, “remove”, and “application/system” suggest conceptual discussions about where security should live (not in obscured source) and how encryption fits.
“journal”, “publisher”, “conference”, “paper”, and “publish” indicate questions about where crypto research is published and how to judge venue/source credibility.

topics.topic_name: Where to start learning crypto (topics and references)
topics.justification: “start”, “understand”, “topic”, “reference”, “search”, and “practice” point to beginner roadmaps and curated lists of what to study first.
With “reference”, “break”, “real_world”, “author”, and “apply”, this topic fits posts citing sources about what breaks in practice and how research claims translate to real use.
“page”, “pdf”, “document”, “website”, “original”, and “line” suggest discussions about locating or reconciling documentation, page numbers, revisions, and exact references.

topics.topic_name: Encryption basics: keys, secrets, and generation
topics.justification: Strong overlap of “key”, “encryption/encrypt”, “secret”, and “generate” indicates conceptual explanations of how encryption uses secrets/keys and how keys are created.
“attack”, “implementation”, “fix”, “time/long/short”, and “package” suggest practical-conceptual discussions about vulnerabilities over time and updating/fixing affected implementations.

topics.topic_name: Performance and runtime trade-offs in crypto
topics.justification: High weights for “fast”, “run”, “time”, and “code” (with some “encryption”) indicate conversations about speed, overhead, and performance implications of cryptographic operations.
“difference”, “broad”, “opinion_base”, and “simple” align with threads asking for high-level comparisons (often subjective) between approaches or concepts.
“message”, “authentication”, and “hash” plus “chapter/resource” fit conceptual explanations of integrity/authentication mechanisms (often HMAC) and pointers to learning material.
Dominated by “book”, “cryptography”, “practical”, “introduction”, and “current”, indicating recommendations for up-to-date introductory/practical texts.

topics.topic_name: Implementing crypto algorithms (don’t roll your own)
topics.justification: “implement/implementation”, “algorithm”, “encryption”, and “break” suggest discussions about the difficulty/risk of implementing cryptography and guidance on safe approaches.
“online”, “free”, “source”, “search”, and “book/cryptography” indicate requests for accessible resources and references available on the web.

topics.topic_name: Public-key cryptography basics (public vs private keys)
topics.justification: “public_key/public”, “private_key”, “random”, and “explain/simple” point to beginner explanations of asymmetric crypto and keypair concepts.
“library”, “code”, “version”, “package”, and “handle” suggest questions about using crypto libraries correctly and dealing with API/packaging/version issues.
“paper”, “nist”, “copy”, and “document” indicate reliance on standards/spec documents (especially NIST) and discussion of specific referenced materials.

topics.topic_name: Choosing standard algorithms for real security
topics.justification: Words like “common”, “standard”, “choose”, “real/security”, and “cryptographic algorithm” suggest guidance on selecting established algorithms rather than ad-hoc schemes.
“learn”, “book”, “math”, “area”, “introduction”, and “suggest/check” indicates beginner learning paths emphasizing the mathematical foundations and recommended starting points.
